opus-5.5.text:
Thanks for having me. I think collaboration at scale is really the central challenge now, more than any single technical idea.

When research was smaller, a few people could own a project end to end: one person had the idea, wrote the code, ran the experiments, and wrote the paper. Building a large foundation model, especially something like a world model for physical AI, doesn't work that way. You need data curation, tokenizers, model architecture, training infrastructure, evaluation, safety, and the downstream robotics or autonomous driving teams who will actually use it. No single person can be an expert in all of that, so the question becomes how to get dozens or hundreds of very smart, opinionated people moving in the same direction.

A few things matter most to me.

First, a clear, shared goal. Researchers are naturally curious and want to explore. That's a strength, but at scale it can scatter effort. So we try to define a concrete target, like a model that can do this capability by this time, and make sure everyone understands why it matters. When people believe in the mission, coordination becomes much easier because they align themselves.

Second, clear ownership with open interfaces. Each sub-team should own its piece, data, the tokenizer, pre-training, post-training, and feel responsible for it. But the boundaries between pieces have to be well defined and transparent, so problems surface early. A lot of failures in big projects happen at the seams, not inside any single component.

Third, credit. This is very important in research culture. In academia, people are used to being first author, and that's how careers are built. In a large project, a contribution might be making the data pipeline ten times faster, which doesn't produce a paper on its own but is absolutely essential. Leaders need to recognize that kind of work publicly and make sure it counts. If people feel only the "glamorous" modeling work is valued, collaboration breaks down quickly.

Fourth, measurement. Fair, agreed-upon evaluation is what lets a big group make decisions without endless debate. If we can test ideas quickly and everyone trusts the benchmark, arguments get settled by evidence rather than seniority or whoever talks loudest.

And finally, I think leaders have to stay hands-on enough to understand the technical details. If you're too far away, you can't make good tradeoff calls, and people can tell. Being close to the work earns trust, and trust is really what makes a large team function.

So for me, it's less about any special management trick and more about building a culture where people feel ownership, feel recognized, and share the same picture of what we're trying to build.

r001.rationale: The response discusses coordination challenges in large teams but does not identify communication demands growing quadratically when every collaborator communicates directly with every other collaborator.

r002.rationale: It says to define a clear, shared goal, ensure everyone understands why it matters, and explains that this helps the team align.

fable-5.1.text:
Thank you for having me. Collaboration at scale is something I think about constantly, because the kind of research we do now, large generative models, world models, simulation, simply cannot be done by one person or even one small team anymore. The days when a brilliant individual could sit alone and produce a breakthrough paper are mostly behind us for this class of problems. You need data people, infrastructure people, training people, evaluation people, and they all have to move in the same direction.

The first thing I would say is that collaboration starts with a shared goal that everyone genuinely believes in. If the goal is vague, people optimize for their own local metric and the pieces never fit together. When I lead a project, I spend a lot of time at the beginning making sure everyone understands not just what we are building, but why it matters and what the end state looks like. Once that is clear, people can make good decisions independently without checking with me every day.

The second thing is trust and giving credit generously. In a large team, the person who fixed the data loader at two in the morning made the result possible just as much as the person who designed the architecture. If credit only flows to a few visible names, the next time you ask for that kind of effort, people will not show up. I try very hard to make sure contributions are visible and that authorship and recognition reflect reality.

The third thing is communication discipline. Large projects fail less often because of bad ideas and more often because two groups were solving the same problem differently without knowing it, or because an assumption changed and nobody told the downstream team. So we keep things simple: regular syncs that are short, a single place where decisions are written down, and a culture where it is completely fine to say "I am blocked" or "I was wrong." Removing the fear of looking bad is probably the single most productive thing a leader can do.

And finally, you have to accept some inefficiency. Coordinating many people has overhead, and if you try to eliminate all of it you end up with a rigid system where nobody can explore. The best teams I have been part of had clear ownership for the core pipeline, but also left room for individuals to try things on the side. Many of our most important ideas came from someone who was not assigned to that problem at all.

r001.rationale: The response discusses communication discipline, but does not identify quadratic growth in communication demands from every collaborator communicating directly with every other collaborator.

r002.rationale: It says collaboration starts with a shared goal everyone understands, and explains that this lets people move in the same direction and make independent decisions.

astra-6.text:
I think the key is to create a shared goal while giving people room to contribute their own ideas. In large-scale AI research, the work is very interconnected. Someone makes a decision about data, and that affects training. Someone changes the model, and that affects the infrastructure. So you need people to understand how their piece connects to the whole project.

That means communicating uncertainty, too. What do we know? What are we assuming? Which experiment would actually help us decide? If people only share successful results, the team loses a lot of valuable information.

And then you need clear ownership. Collaboration doesn’t mean everyone has to be involved in every decision. People should know what they’re responsible for and who they can ask for help. Ideally, you have enough structure to move together, and enough freedom for someone to surprise you with a better idea.

r001.rationale: The response discusses interconnected work and coordination, but does not identify quadratic growth in direct communication demands as a scaling problem.

r002.rationale: It recommends creating a shared goal and helping people understand how their work connects to the whole project, communicating goal alignment across the team.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the key is to make sure people share an understanding of the problem, while giving them room to contribute their own expertise. In a large team, you can divide the work, but you still need a common picture of what success looks like and how the pieces fit together.

That means being explicit about assumptions, sharing results early, and making it easy to discuss what isn’t working. A negative result can save another team weeks of effort, but only if people feel comfortable sharing it.

And credit matters. Large-scale AI research depends on many contributions—ideas, data, infrastructure, experiments. When those contributions are recognized, people have a stronger reason to help one another succeed.

r001.rationale: The response discusses collaboration practices but does not identify all-to-all communication or its quadratic growth as a scaling problem.

r002.rationale: It says a large team needs a shared understanding of the problem and a common picture of success, communicating goal clarity as a way to align the team.
